overview: The imperial Rashtrakutas made the Deccan a major center of power between the eighth and tenth centuries. Their world included formidable armies, Kannada literature, schools and extraordinary stone carving. This map’s 800 to 1000 window is approximate: the dynasty rose earlier, and its imperial rule collapsed around 973, before the outline disappears.

periods.title: Imperial expansion
periods.summary: The empire inherited the conquests of Dantidurga and Krishna I and sent armies beyond the Deccan.

periods.title: Learning and patronage
periods.summary: Amoghavarsha’s literary patronage forms part of a wider world of mathematical scholarship.

periods.title: Schools and contested kingship
periods.summary: The Salotgi donation documents learning during Krishna III’s reign.

periods.title: After imperial rule
periods.summary: Taila II overthrew Karka II; the map continues beyond that political change.

items.text: Dantidurga broke the supremacy of the Badami Chalukyas, and his uncle Krishna I continued the conquests. The empire grew through campaigns and the submission of other rulers. A large colored area on a map cannot show the changing bargains between an emperor and the chiefs beneath him.

A copper-plate grant issued by Govinda III in 808 names Ambakagram, a village granted to Damodarabhatta, a Brahman from Vengi. Such documents join distant places and named people in one transaction. For historians, these durable records can be more useful than a king’s enormous claims about his own glory.

Amoghavarsha I is associated with Kavirajamarga, an early surviving work on Kannada poetics. His precise role is described as author or inspiration in the state gazetteer. Supporting literature could bring a ruler lasting fame quite different from the fame earned by marching an army across someone else’s fields.

A charter of 926 praises Madhumati, an Arab governor of Samyana, usually identified with Sanjan. The Sanskrit name represents Muhammad. It describes a ruler serving Rashtrakuta kings while administering coastal territory: the empire’s officials did not all share one ancestry or religious background.

That charter records free ferries across two streams and a feeding house serving rice, curries and ghee. This is a rare glimpse of an actual public meal, rather than a modern guess at a medieval menu. A traveler could benefit from both the crossing and the cooking.

Another part of the same record grants a village to maintain a religious establishment built by Annaiya and provide offerings to a goddess. Farming income helped support buildings and services. Land grants therefore mattered to cultivators as well as to the officials who signed them.

At Salotgi, an inscription connected with a donation in 945 describes a school established by Narayana, Krishna III’s minister. It welcomed scholars from different regions. The named institution was a religious learning community; the inscription does not describe universal schooling for every child.

The school’s support included twenty-seven dwelling places, land for a flower garden and land whose income paid for lamps. More land and a dwelling supported the teacher. Even a medieval school needed a budget for the unglamorous business of keeping people housed and the lights on.

Families contributed during marriages, thread-investiture ceremonies and ritual hair cutting. The inscription sets different contributions for these occasions. School support was woven into important events in the local Brahman community’s life, rather than relying on a single royal present.

The Kailasanatha temple at Ellora, associated with Krishna I, represents Shiva’s mountain home. Although it looks like a constructed temple, its great forms were carved from the rock. The British Library’s catalogue of an old drawing identifies the separate Nandi pavilion and the temple’s sacred setting.

Stonecutters isolated a block by cutting three trenches into the hillside. Teams worked on the main tower, gateway and other parts of the complex. Making rooms and columns by removing rock required planning in three dimensions. This was a building project in which taking material away created the architecture.

Ellora also preserves Buddhist and Jain monuments, created across several centuries. A smaller Jain temple, Chhota Kailasa, adapted the great temple’s monolithic design. Sharing an artistic method did not require sharing the same sacred images: neighboring communities could recognize a good architectural idea.

A famous Ellora relief shows Ravana attempting to lift Shiva’s mountain. Surviving paintings on ceilings remind us that the monuments were not simply bare gray stone. Sculptors and painters used dramatic stories to make sacred places vivid for their visitors.

Around 850, the Jain scholar Mahavira organized a mathematical handbook into subjects including fractions, areas, excavations and shadows. It used place-value numerals. These topics connect calculation to measuring land and spaces as well as to puzzles: numbers could help people picture and manage the physical world.

Mahavira also worked with permutations and combinations, ways of counting arrangements and selections. His introduction, preserved in a university account, describes mathematics as useful in ordinary affairs as well as learned subjects. Rashtrakuta-era intellectual achievement included this patient work of finding rules, not only spectacular royal monuments.

The Salotgi school inscription opens “Svasti śrīḥ”, translated by its editors as “Hail! Fortune!” This is Sanskrit in scholarly Roman transcription from the 945 record, originally carved in an early Kannada script. The greeting leads into praise, dates and the practical arrangements for supporting scholars.

ending.text: Taila II of the Chalukyas overthrew Karka II around 973. The imperial court lost power, but the region’s communities, learning and monuments continued. The imported outline lasts to 1000; that later boundary is not the date of a further Rashtrakuta empire’s collapse.
